deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematics: no formulas or derivations, only historical and motivational prose. It is page 18 of the fair copy of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Ueber die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854; published posthumously by Dedekind in 1867, Abh. Ges. Wiss. Göttingen 13). It belongs to the historical part (§§1–3) and continues the argument of the previous page.

(1) The previous page explained that Dirichlet's 1829 theorem settles every case occurring in nature. This page gives the first reason why the cases Dirichlet left open still deserve study: the subject is closely tied to the principles of the infinitesimal calculus and can bring those principles to 'greater clarity and definiteness'. The answer therefore has direct foundational interest.

(2) The second reason is that Fourier series are no longer confined to physics. They have been applied successfully in pure mathematics, namely number theory, and there precisely the functions whose representability Dirichlet did not examine seem important. Two details:
- 'Fou-' is struck out before 'trigonometrische Reihe'.
- The number-theoretic applications are presumably Dirichlet's own: Gauss sums, the class-number formula, primes in progressions. Riemann gives no specific functions here. My guess is that he has in mind sawtooth-type functions such as ((x)) and sums like Σ((nx))/n², which he treats later in §6; they have infinitely many discontinuities, which falls outside Dirichlet's hypotheses.

(3) Dirichlet promised at the end of his memoir to return to these cases, but the promise is still unfulfilled.

(4) The works of Dirksen and Bessel on cosine and sine series do not fill the gap; they are inferior to Dirichlet's in rigour and generality.
- Dirksen's paper (Crelle's Journal 4, 1829, p. 170) is almost simultaneous with Dirichlet's and evidently written without knowledge of it. It takes a generally correct path but contains inaccuracies:
  - In a special case (his formula 22) it gives a wrong value for the sum of the series.
  - In a side argument (Art. 3) it relies on a series expansion possible only in special cases.
  - Hence its proof is complete only for functions whose first derivative is finite everywhere.
- Bessel (Schumacher's Astronomische Nachrichten No. 374, Bd. 16, p. 229, 1839) tries to simplify Dirichlet's proof. The critique continues on the next page: his changes give no real simplification of the reasoning and only dress it in more familiar concepts, at a considerable cost in rigour and generality.

No computation is performed. The page serves as motivation for Riemann's programme: treat representability without assuming Dirichlet's conditions (integrability, finitely many maxima and minima). That programme leads into §4 on the definite integral (the Riemann integral).
errors: No mathematical errors: the page contains no derivations. Its historical claims (Dirichlet's unfulfilled promise; Dirksen 1829 being nearly simultaneous with Dirichlet 1829; Bessel 1839 in AN 16) agree with the published text and with standard history.

results.what: Motivation for studying the cases Dirichlet left open: foundations of the calculus, and number-theoretic applications of Fourier series to functions with infinitely many discontinuities
results.modern_name: Historical introduction to the Riemann Habilitationsschrift (representability of functions by trigonometric series)

results.what: Critique of Dirksen (1829): wrong sum in a special case (his formula 22), proof complete only for functions with bounded/finite derivative; critique of Bessel (1839) as less rigorous than Dirichlet

deep.surprise_reason: This is the well-known, published historical introduction (§3) of Riemann's 1854 Habilitationsschrift. It contains no mathematics beyond historical commentary that has been in print since 1867.

checkable.asserts: Context check, not on this page: a Fourier coefficient of the sawtooth ((x)) = x - 1/2 on (0,1), with ((x)) = -sum sin(2 pi n x)/(pi n), the kind of function used in number theory and discussed later by Riemann; should simplify to 0 with the factor 2 accounted for (coefficient b_1 = 2*integral = -1/pi).
